summary:
ORBITAL is an offline health-monitoring app for astronauts on long-duration missions, designed to be easy to use, visually clear and quick to complete in a busy schedule. It brings together data from onboard medical devices, a wearable (simulated in our demo), short self-reports on mood, sleep and symptoms, and quick in-app tests for reaction time (PVT) and vision (Amsler grid). Every indicator is linked to an official NASA Human Research Program risk, and its thresholds come from NASA-STD-3001 and other cited clinical sources.

ORBITAL compares each reading with clinical thresholds and with the astronaut’s own baseline. Results appear on a color-coded body figure, each with a plain-language next step: keep the routine, watch and self-care, consult the onboard medical officer, or escalate to the flight surgeon on Earth.

On a Mars mission, communication delays of up to 20 minutes each way mean crews can’t count on Earth in real time. ORBITAL gives astronauts understanding of, and agency over, their own health. It never replaces medicine: it guides, it does not diagnose, and it makes sure the right professional is involved at the right time.
details:
What does it do?
ORBITAL is a health-monitoring app for astronauts on long-duration missions. It aims to be easy to use, visually clear, and quick enough to fit into a busy crew schedule. Each day the astronaut enters values from medical devices already on board and completes short check-in scales, such as mood and fatigue. The app also runs quick tests of its own: a psychomotor vigilance test (PVT) for reaction time and an Amsler grid for vision changes. A continuous wearable modeled on the CSA’s Bio-Monitor/Astroskin adds more data, which is simulated in the demo.

ORBITAL tracks blood pressure, resting heart rate, SpO₂, glucose, sleep hours, reaction time, mood and fatigue, vision, cumulative radiation dose and cabin CO₂. Each indicator is linked to an official NASA Human Research Program risk, such as cardiovascular adaptations, inadequate sleep, behavioral conditions, SANS, radiation and hypoxia.

How does it work?

  1. Input: device readings, check-in scales, in-app tests and wearable data (simulated)
    • 🟢 Green: within expected range, keep the routine.
    • 🟡 Yellow: sustained drift from the personal baseline, or a borderline value. A soft alert asks the astronaut to watch, re-measure and take care of themselves.
    • 🟠 Orange: out of clinical range, or a marked and sustained deviation. Consult the onboard medical officer.
    • 🔴 Red: critical value. Escalate to the flight surgeon on Earth with a ready-to-send report.
  2. Output: a clickable human body figure colored by body system, trend charts, and a plain-language explanation with a next step for each result.

Everything runs on board, with no connection to Earth.

What benefits does it have?

  • It empowers the astronaut: results come in plain language with a clear next step, so astronauts understand their own health and can act on it.
  • It respects medicine: ORBITAL guides, it does not diagnose. It never replaces the onboard medical officer or the flight surgeon. Instead it makes sure the right professional is involved at the right time.
  • Autonomy: on a Mars mission, communication delays of up to 20 minutes each way mean crews can’t rely on Earth in real time. ORBITAL makes the first call on board.
  • Personalization: each astronaut is compared with themselves, not only with population ranges. NASA’s Standard Measures program and the ESA/NASA Venous Haemostasis study both show that individual responses to spaceflight vary.
  • One clear view: NASA and the CSA already measure these signals, but in separate sessions, and much of the analysis happens on Earth. ORBITAL brings them together in one picture that is easy to read.

What is the intended impact?
We see ORBITAL as a prototype of the onboard clinical decision support NASA describes for exploration missions. A “Space passenger” profile extends the same approach to commercial spaceflight participants, who have less medical training and less ground support.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Python 3.11 with pandas, numpy and pytest
  • FastAPI + React / TypeScript
  • Interface screens prototyped with Google AI Studio
  • A data simulator based on figures published by NASA and the CSA
  • AI-assisted development with human oversight: Claude (chat and Claude Code) for research, organizing work, coding and documentation. The team reviewed all code and clinical content.
  • No custom hardware: the app is designed to work with devices and wearables that already exist on board.

How is it creative?
Most monitoring tools show numbers or send them to the ground. ORBITAL interprets them on board against each astronaut’s own baseline, presents them visually, and turns each result into a four-level path toward the right person. It also combines physiological data with cognitive and psychological tests that take seconds (PVT, Amsler grid, check-in scales), so the crew can catch early changes between formal medical checks.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Clinical validity: every threshold has a cited source, and team proposals are marked as proposals. One team member has a clinical (kinesiology) background.
  • Usability: short tasks, clear visuals and plain language for a crew with limited time.
  • Safety and ethics: the app guides and does not diagnose. All demo data is simulated and declared as such.
  • Real constraints: no connection to Earth, limited time and limited onboard equipment.
  • Scope: we prioritized a working, well-tested rules engine over adding more features.

Future work: anomaly-detection layer (proposal, not implemented)
The current engine looks at one measurement at a time, so it can miss several small changes that happen together. For example, heart rate slightly up, sleep slightly shorter, fatigue slightly higher and SpO₂ slightly lower on the same days. Each value stays green on its own, but together they could be an early sign of poor sleep, CO₂ build-up or an infection.

We designed an unsupervised layer that would learn what is normal for each astronaut and flag that kind of combined pattern. It would run alongside the rules without replacing them, cap its alerts at yellow, always explain which measurements raised the score, and switch on in stages as each astronaut’s history grows. We did not build a supervised risk model on purpose: that would need real astronaut data with clinical outcomes, which is not publicly available. Trained on our simulated data, it would only learn back the rules we wrote. The full proposal is in our README.

Other next steps: bone and exercise load, nutrition, immune signals, motion sickness and team-dynamics scales.

Source code
Our full code and documentation are on GitHub: https://github.com/paulinaguers/orbital
We think it’s important to share the repository in addition to the demo. The demo shows how ORBITAL looks and feels, while the repository shows how it works: the processing engine, the clinical thresholds with their sources, the data simulator, the tests, the ML proposal and our development log.
